description:
How can you protect yourself from the Dajjal, and the era of dajalah (deception) that comes before him? 

The Prophet ﷺ gave us guidance for our protection from these trials, including multiple du’as and 20 verses from Surah al-Kahf — and he taught us to make sure that we don’t become agents of deception today.  

Here is a du’a he ﷺ taught us for when we leave home every day: 

اللّهُـمَّ إِنِّـي أَعـوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَضِـلَّ أَوْ أُضَـل أَوْ أَزِلَّ أَوْ أُزَل أَوْ أَظْلِـمَ أَوْ أَُظْلَـم أَوْ أَجْهَلَ أَوْ يُـجْهَلَ عَلَـيّ

Allahumma 'inni 'aʿudhu bika 'an 'adilla, 'aw 'udalla, 'aw 'azilla, 'aw 'uzalla, 'aw 'adhlima, 'aw 'udhlama, 'aw 'ajhala 'aw yujhala ʿalayya.

O Allah, I seek refuge in You lest I misguide others, or I am misguided by others, lest I cause others to err or I am caused to err, lest I abuse others or be abused, and lest I behave foolishly or meet with the foolishness of others.

[Abu Dawud, hadith no. 5075]

And a du’a to read at the end of your salah:

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ عَذَابِ جَهَنَّمَ وَمِنْ عَذَابِ الْقَبْرِ وَمِنْ فِتْنَةِ الْمَحْيَا وَالْمَمَاتِ وَمِنْ شَرِّ فِتْنَةِ الْمَسِيحِ الدَّجَّالِ

Allahumma inni aʿudhu bika min ‘adhabi jahannama, wa-min ʿadhabi-l-qabri, wa-min fitnati-l-mahya wa-l-mamati, wa-min sharri fitnati-l-masihi-d-dajjal.

O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of Hell, from the punishment of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the evil trial of the False Messiah.

[Sahih Muslim, hadith

description:

What if one sentence could erase your entire record?

On Laylatul Qadr, our mother Aisha (RA) did not ask for a list. She asked one question. The Prophet (PBUH) did not give her a ladder to climb or a prayer to memorize. He gave her one name of Allah, one attribute, and one ask: O Allah, You are Al-'Afuww, the Pardoner. You love to pardon. So pardon me.

In this episode, Dr. Omar Suleiman draws a clear line between Al-Maghfirah, forgiveness, and Al-'Afuww, pardon. Forgiveness covers a sin and protects you from its consequence. Pardon removes the trace entirely, as if the sin never existed. The scholars describe it as a wind sweeping the desert floor so that not even a footprint remains. That is the level of mercy this supplication is reaching for, and it is available to anyone who asks with a sincere heart on Laylatul Qadr.

The story of Abu Bakr (RA) and his relative Mustah brings this out of theology and into real life. Mustah was someone Abu Bakr financially supported, and he was among those who slandered the Prophet's wife, Aisha (RA). When Abu Bakr found out, he cut off the support. Allah then revealed a verse asking whether Abu Bakr would not love for Allah to pardon him. Abu Bakr did not just forgive Mustah. He restored everything he had been giving him, as if nothing had ever happened. That is what Al-'Afuww looks like when it lives inside a person.

title: Why We Pray Five Times a Day
description:
Most people treat prayer like another task squeezed into an already crowded day. Something to get through quickly before returning to everything else demanding attention.

But salah was never meant to compete with your life. It was meant to interrupt it.

Throughout the day, responsibilities pile up, conversations pull your focus, and worries slowly fill the mind. Without noticing it, the heart begins to revolve entirely around the world.

Salah breaks that cycle.

Five times a day, everything pauses. The schedule stops, the noise fades, and you step away from people, obligations, and distractions to stand before the One who gave you the day itself.

Those few minutes are not a burden on your time. They are a mercy placed within it.

Because a heart left in the dunya all day begins to suffocate. And salah is the moment Allah gives you to breathe again.

title: Where Patience Shows Up in Your Life
description:
Most people imagine patience as one moment of restraint. A single decision to stay calm when something difficult happens.

But sabr isn’t just one reaction. It quietly appears across different parts of a believer’s life.

Sometimes patience shows up when you walk away from a temptation you could easily have taken. Sometimes it appears in hardship, when pain doesn’t turn you bitter or reckless. Other times it’s the quiet consistency of continuing a good deed long after the motivation fades.

Patience is also what allows a person to rebuild after failure instead of staying down. It’s the ability to start again after a mistake, a loss, or a disappointment.

And perhaps the hardest form of patience is the patience we show people. The restraint we practice when others frustrate us, misunderstand us, or test our limits.

Remembering how patient Allah has been with us often makes that last one easier.

title: The True Healer
description:
We live in a time where healing feels almost entirely mechanical. You feel pain, you see a doctor, you receive treatment, and if things improve the credit usually goes to the medicine or the procedure.

Islam doesn’t reject any of those means. In fact, it encourages us to seek them. But it quietly corrects the way the heart understands them. A doctor can diagnose, prescribe, and treat, but the ability for a body to recover was never in their hands to begin with.

Every recovery, every closing wound, every fever that breaks, and every illness that lifts happens only because Allah allows the body to heal.

That’s why the Prophet ﷺ taught us to ask Allah as Ash-Shaafy, the One who heals completely. Not the One who merely reduces pain for a moment, but the One who can restore entirely and remove harm in ways no medicine can guarantee.

So the believer takes the means seriously, but the heart never attaches itself to the means. The prescription may be in the doctor’s hand, but healing itself remains with Allah.
